#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Extends resource_execution_seconds with additional dimensions so that with metrics only it's easier to tell which calls are causing priority level saturation.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/109108

issue_context.title: Improve observability of execution latency in APF
issue_context.body:
### What would you like to be added?

When I debug some slow API calls where API Priority and Fairness started throttling requests, it's often hard to tell which requests are in fact throttled due to priority level being throttled vs simply being slow. We have added already fl_priorityandfairness which shows how much time we have spent on waiting for request to start, but it is still harder than it should be to find requests with significant (latency-fl_priorityandfairness) latency.

Proposal:
* Add apf_execution_latency with "real" time we have spent on executing the API call
* Add verb, resource, group dimensions to existing request_execution_seconds metric to provide some insights based only on metrics.

/sig api-machinery

/cc @wojtek-t 
/cc @MikeSpreitzer 
/cc @tkashem 

### Why is this needed?

To make API call latency incidents debuggable.

review_comments: If we add these, we need the same guards put in place to prevent unbounded values that we have on other metrics

[I'm not suggesting to ignore this problem - just asking question]
There are still metrics where we don't do anything, right? the core requestCounter metrics is one of those where IIUC we just put everything as is, right?
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/metrics/metrics.go#L436

Why is that one non-problematic? @dgrisonnet

As far as I am aware, the only metrics that have these labels are the ones used to compute the kube-apiserver SLOs. So `kube_apiserver_request_total` and `kube_apiserver_request_duration`.

These ones are actually problematic, we are talking about metrics that represent around 50% of the timeseries exposed by the apiserver. Over the years, there have been many complaints about these metrics resulting in too many series, but most of them were discarded as these metrics are essential to know the apiserver's availability.

So I would say that these metrics are problematic, but because of their importance, we lived with the memory impact that they could bring and I don't think any other metrics are important enough to justify this cost.

That said, we might want to consider changing that. Bounding the number of resources values exposed doesn't sound like a bad idea. Even more since we have added latency information to the audit logs (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/107910). With that, even if we get rid of most of the resource-level information, we would still be able to get it from the audit logs.

Going even further with that idea, if one was to hide all the resource-level information today (e.g dropping the labels at ingestion), it wouldn't impact the SLO computation since it isn't required there, and they would still be able to investigate issues at a resource-level from the logs. So I think that we might be able to make nice memory gains by introducing a resource allowlist for these metrics.

> So I would say that these metrics are problematic, but because of their importance, we lived with the memory impact that they could bring and I don't think any other metrics are important enough to justify this cost.

OK - that makes sense to me.

> Going even further with that idea, if one was to hide all the resource-level information today (e.g dropping the labels at ingestion), it wouldn't impact the SLO computation since it isn't required there, and they would still be able to investigate issues at a resource-level from the logs. So I think that we might be able to make nice memory gains by introducing a resource allowlist for these metrics.

I disagree with this one. We're defining SLO per (resource, verb) pair: https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/sig-scalability/slos/api_call_latency.md so unless I misunderstood something I don't think we will be able to compute it. And I don't think we should be going towards computing SLOs from audit logs.
Also note - that audit logs don't contain all the requests - IIRC even the default policies remove some system-originating (read) requests, which we really want to have in SLOs. We may try doing a bit of bundling, but I don't agree we can actually drop the labels.

So as long as I agree we shouldn't be adding more metrics with such high cardinality, I don't really agree we are ready to drop labels from the two you mentioned above.

I was slightly wrong, I forgot that we are using the subresource label for SLOs: https://github.com/kubernetes/perf-tests/blob/master/clusterloader2/pkg/measurement/common/slos/api_responsiveness_prometheus.go#L48. But, I don't think we are using the resource label at all there. We are not defining SLO threshold based on each resource latency, but rather based on their scope since that is where we can see big differences. The subresource filter is just here to handle a few corner cases.

I can see how useful these labels are today, but I can also see a potential world without any values for them, or only a few allow listed ones in order to reduce costs.

> Also note - that audit logs don't contain all the requests - IIRC even the default policies remove some system-originating (read) requests, which we really want to have in SLOs. We may try doing a bit of bundling, but I don't agree we can actually drop the labels.

We won't be able to drop the labels from the codebase anyway since the metrics are stable, but we might still be able to filter them.
I wasn't aware that some requests are not present in the audit logs. As I mentioned before, I don't think how SLOs are computed will be impacted, but if we start filtering some resources, we might be dropping the only information we have about these requests which might be problematic.

> But, I don't think we are using the resource label at all there. We are not defining SLO threshold based on each resource latency, but rather based on their scope since that is where we can see big differences. The subresource filter is just here to handle a few corner cases.

No - the SLO is per (resource, verb) pair. So each (resource, verb) has to be satisfied on your own (see the definition I linked above).

Ah yes, you are right, I missed that. So I guess all the resource values are required to compute the SLOs in the scalability tests. However, if we want to alert based on the SLOs given by sig-scalability, I don't think that is the case. There is only one error budget for the apiserver, not one per resource, and since the latency thresholds calculated by sig-scalability are defined at the scope level, we will end up not needing any resource-level information to setup burn rate alerts.

For dashboards it might be a bit different since having more granularity is always better, but reducing the number of resource values to only critical resources doesn't sound that bad. Cluster admins would be able to see if anything critical is impacted right away and if not they could always dig deeper into the log to figure out which resource is impacted.

The tradeoff of having to go through logs in some cases instead of having everything into the metrics for some memory gains doesn't sound like a bad option to give to users.

> There is only one error budget for the apiserver, not one per resource, and since the latency thresholds calculated by sig-scalability are defined at the scope level, we will end up not needing any resource-level information to setup burn rate alerts.

I don't agree. You can define many other SLOs for kube-apiserver (e.g. availability SLO,  etc.) so talking about "single-error budget per kube-apiserver", it not a correct thinking.
Technically - you can think about the current latency SLO not as a single SLO, but rather as multiple different SLO: 1. SLO for "POST pods", 2. SLO for "PATCH pods", 3. SLO for GET pod, ....
So if you want to measure those SLOs in production - you need all the information that current exists.

You may argue that we should redefine the SLO - we were having this discussion multiple times already (shouldn't we merge the SLO into less streams) and for now sticked to it for multiple reasons (including the fact that certain calls may be implemented visible different than others (e.g. create/delete service are such operations) and if those are very rare, we just don't want to loose them among others.

> The tradeoff of having to go through logs in some cases instead of having everything into the metrics for some memory gains doesn't sound like a bad option to give to users.

If you have a cluster that generates thousands of QPS, then unless you don't know exactly what you're looking for (which is usually from metrics) - logs aren't super helpful - or they are extremely time consuming.
does this start to cause the same cardinality issues as with the other request metric?
